stimulus.text: Paraphrase of standard accounts of three sisters agriculture: maize, beans, and squash were planted together in the same field. Tall maize stalks held climbing bean vines. Broad squash leaves spread across the ground below, shading the soil. Together the three crops fed dense, settled populations in eastern North America.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of standard accounts; see grounding.

stem: In the three sisters system, tall maize stalks rise above climbing bean vines while broad squash leaves spread across the ground below. This arrangement best illustrates which feature of Native American agriculture?

options.text: Planting a single crop across enormous cleared fields to raise the harvest yield.
options.misconception: Describes monoculture, the opposite of interplanting three crops.

options.text: Combining crops so that each uses a different layer of the growing space.
Leaving fields unplanted for years at a time to rest the soil.
options.misconception: Describes leaving land idle, not planting crops together.

options.text: Clearing forests with European iron axes and saws brought from Spain.
options.misconception: Credits European tools for a pre-contact Native system.

rationales.A: A single crop across huge fields is monoculture, the opposite of planting three crops together.
rationales.B: Maize grows tall, beans climb the stalks, and squash covers the ground, so three crops share one field by layer.
rationales.C: The system is about planting together, not about leaving land unplanted for years.
rationales.D: Three sisters farming was a pre-contact Native system, developed without European axes and saws.
rationales.general:
1. Picture the field as a three-story house. Maize stands tall, beans climb the stalks, and squash spreads below.
2. Name the pattern. Three crops share one field by using different layers, roof, stairs, and floor.
3. Ask what sharing gains. Each layer catches light and space the others do not use.
4. Name the method. That stacking is interplanting, the heart of three sisters farming.
Remember: when crops share a field, ask how each one uses a different part of the space.
